facts.title: OUR STRATEGIC PLAN
facts.body:
Our Strategic Plan - Vision, Purpose Statement, Guiding Principles and Commitments - reflect what stakeholders told us - what they value and aspire to for Charlottetown.

The core elements of Our Plan are designed to complement and reinforce each other and should be considered as a whole.

Our Vision

Respecting the past. Embracing the future. Creating a community for everyone.

Our Purpose

As a local level of government, the City of Charlottetown is committed to:

Delivering community-focused programs and services that matter most to our residents.

Specifically, we will:

provide accountable, accessible and fiscally responsive local government to build a sustainable and resilient city; and,

approach challenges and problem-solving with innovation and integrity, by reflecting solutions that serve the whole community.

facts.title: PILLARS
facts.body:
The four pillars are areas that represent the major parts of city life and require transformational change over the next four years and beyond.

These include:

•   Community-Building and Placemaking

•   Governance and Civic Engagement

•   Inclusive Economic Growth

•   Infrastructure and the Environment

Each pillar has a number of focus areas. These identify the specific ways the pillars will be used to develop and manage the Action Plan over the life of our Strategic Plan. These pillars will guide strategic thinking about Charlottetown now and into the future.

In practice, no pillar should be considered in isolation to the others, or to the guiding principles and commitments established for the plan. They are about Charlottetown in the future – reflecting some of what the City is today but also incorporating the vision for the future – what residents and leaders want it to become tomorrow.

facts.title: Community-Building and Placemaking
facts.body:
To enhance Charlottetown as a great place to live and as a destination for visitors. We will:

• Prioritize waterfront development and expanding the waterfront’s footprint and amenities to continue to enhance its

attractiveness as a destination while being anticipatory of requirements related to preparation for sea level rise and related environmental considerations. Building opportunities for residents and visitors to experience its waterways.

• Create a multicultural city that is welcoming to both new residents and newcomers and which celebrates and honours

the diversity of its people and their traditions.

• Take a ‘whole of Charlottetown’ perspective on planning which addresses environmental considerations, including

‘density’, while creating a city-of- neighbourhoods, bringing residents closer to the services they need and the lifestyle and leisure options they want, enhancing livability, walkability and the reduction of GHGs.

• Enhance connectivity to support investment attraction, attraction of immigrants and in migration and to enhance hybrid

work capacity; and,

• Leverage the potential of all lands within the City.

facts.title: Governance and Civic Engagement
facts.body:
To create a high performance and responsive local government. We will:

• Model fiscal sustainability and transparency within an enhanced accountability framework through the Action Plan

accompanying this strategic plan.

• Develop new systems to strengthen annual monitoring to enhance the accountability framework.

• Prioritize people and safety to help strengthen our community and quality of life.

• Serve as leaders in creating a culture of community safety by protecting people, property and the environment.

• Develop the opportunity for shared services with adjoining municipalities where there is a business case to do so.

• Provide enhanced community-centric government balancing the needs of neighbourhoods while taking a

‘whole of Charlottetown’ planning perspective.

• Develop a decision-making template that incorporates the guiding principles outlined in this plan as a filter to support

all decision making related to by-law, policy and regulatory changes; and,

• Grow the use of technology to support citizen engagement and

streamlined accessibility to municipal processes.

facts.title: Inclusive Economic Growth
facts.body:
To foster inclusive growth related in terms of people and our economic sectors. We will:

• Continue to focus on population growth by attracting new residents whether through immigration or in-migration from

other communities on- and- off Island, including continued efforts to ensure a welcoming community, provide necessary settlement services for newcomers and measures to enhance immigrant retention.

• Advance reconciliation efforts along with positioning Charlottetown as a welcoming city.

• Work with other public and private partners to address innovative solutions to housing including facilitating a

streamlined regulatory and approval process designed to facilitate development.

• Collaborate with other levels of government and leverage its partnered organizations - Charlottetown Area

Development Corporation, Discover Charlottetown, Downtown Charlottetown Inc., arts and cultural organizations and the innovation ecosystem – to support investment attraction and foster inclusive growth; and,

• Approach municipal support for cultural, artistic, tourist, sport hosting and event-related activities as investments

with accompanying economic and social impacts for the benefit of residents and visitors alike.

facts.title: Infrastructure and the Environment
facts.body:
To address infrastructure challenges in our growing city and the issues arising from climate change adaptation and mitigation. We will:

• Set priorities for greening all its infrastructure in a planned and orderly manner through the new Official Plan.

• Make sustainability, community resilience and climate change management and mitigation foundational criteria on

which to base all infrastructure investment decisions.

• Continue to respect, preserve and enhance heritage assets while also embracing the principle of adaptive re-use and

the circular economy.

• Enhance accessibility to information and data to guide decision making and provide information citizens require through

investment in smart infrastructure, technology and tools, such as GIS; and,

• Ensure that planning for and accommodating population growth optimizes both land use and the

need for additional / expanded infrastructure.

guides.title: How a municipal budget is prepared
guides.body: A municipal budget is an annual financial plan. Administration and departments estimate the cost of maintaining services, identify proposed changes, and prepare operating and capital plans. Council reviews the plans, may amend them, and adopts the final budget through the municipality's required public process.

guides.title: Operating budget
guides.body: The operating budget covers recurring services and day-to-day municipal activities. It records expected revenue and expenses for the fiscal period, including staffing, utilities, maintenance, public safety, administration, grants, fees, taxes, and transfers.

guides.title: Capital budget
guides.body: The capital budget covers long-lived assets and major projects. It separates gross project cost, external or partner funding, financing, and the net municipal amount. A capital allocation authorizes a budget; it does not establish that the money has already been spent.

guides.title: How municipal budgets are funded
guides.body: Municipal funding commonly combines property taxes, user rates and fees, grants and transfers, reserve funds, and borrowing. The available sources and legal rules vary by municipality and jurisdiction. Source-specific rates, assessments, grants, debt, and funding deductions remain separate from this general explanation.

facts.title: About Charlottetown
facts.body:
Serving as the capital city of Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown is known as the "Birthplace of Confederation" due to the historic 1864 Charlottetown Conference that paved the way for Confederation. Dynamic and sustainable, our scenic waterfront city serves as the seat of government and is a vibrant hub of culture and education.

With its burgeoning knowledge economy and strategic location, Charlottetown attracts global businesses in diverse sectors including biotechnology, financial services, information technology, and manufacturing. Supported by a skilled workforce and a favorable business environment, the City's key sectors drive economic growth and innovation.

Charlottetown offers an unparalleled quality of life, featuring a blend of big city amenities, cultural events, and recreational opportunities within a safe, clean environment characterized by a strong sense of community. As a major tourism destination and designated Cultural Capital of Canada, Charlottetown hosts year-round attractions such as the renowned Charlottetown Festival and serves as a venue for high-quality meetings and conventions. Moreover, Charlottetown has emerged as a prominent sport sport tourism destination, boasting state-of-the-art sports facilities and hosting major sporting events throughout the year.

With its rich history, diverse and vibrant culture, thriving economy, and exceptional quality of life, Charlottetown continues to attract residents, businesses, visitors, and sports enthusiasts from around the globe.

Land Acknowledgement

In the spirit of Reconciliation, we acknowledge that the land upon which we gather is unceded Mi’kmaq territory. Epekwitk (Prince Edward Island), Mi’kma’ki, is covered by the historic Treaties of Peace and

Friendship. We pay our respects to the Indigenous

Mi’kmaq People who have occupied this Island for over 12,000 years; past, present and future.

facts.title: Finance Committee chair's introduction
facts.body:
Introduction from the Chair of the Finance,

Audit, Tendering and Administration Committee

This year’s budget process has been a little bit different to any other we’ve gone through. For example, this has been the most transparent budget that we have engaged in as a City. Every meeting that could be held in an open session and livestreamed to our YouTube channel was held in open and recorded. Every debate, every question, every priority was brought to the forefront for public consumption; you, the taxpayer, were able to watch a realistic approach to planning the next fiscal year as it happened.

Last fall, members of Council met with senior City staff to identify a strategic direction and set clear priorities for the upcoming budget. We were fortunate to have the Community Survey results to provide an in- depth review of what our community prioritises and, combined with what we heard through conversations with residents, we were prepared for the

weeks of discussions and reviews that budget always brings. We also considered forecasts and global economic trends as we approved the planned projects and initiatives that can realistically be completed during the fiscal year.

An unescapable fact is that Charlottetown continues to grow. We’re excited for the opportunities growth brings but mindful of the investment required to maintain, update and build new infrastructure, to improve our facilities and to increase services. We knew this budget had to reflect our community’s focus on increasing feelings of safety, so policing features prominently. It also contains a small increase in Water and Sewer rates to help maintain our infrastructure and cover rising administrative costs. As you look through this budget book, I’m confident that you’ll see an appropriate balance in addressing urgent capital and operational needs; that balance is the result of months of hard work. The figures tell the story of a strategic approach to prioritizing projects and initiatives to be prudent and responsible while enabling ongoing investments to continue sustainably preparing for the growth of our City while maintaining the excellent quality of life you deserve.

Councillor John McAleer

Legislative Framework

The City of Charlottetown engages in a comprehensive budget preparation process to allocate resources effectively. In doing so the City must adhere to the Municipal Government Act of Prince Edward Island (the Act) and the Financial Plan Regulations (the Regulations). The Act and Regulations set out the rules for how the City must handle its money, including budgeting, planning for future expenses, and keeping track of assets. The legislation refers to the City budget as a Financial Plan.

Key legislative requirements from the Act:

The fiscal year for the City is April 1 to March 31 [S149(1)]

On or before March 31 in each year, City Council shall by resolution adopt a budget for the upcoming fiscal year. [S150(2)]

The budget must include an operating budget, capital budget, and a 5-year capital expenditure program that includes an asset management program. [ S150(2)]

City Council must provide public notice and hold a public meeting regarding the budget not less than two weeks before it receives final approval and is adopted. [S151(1)]

A copy of the final approved budget shall be filed with the Minister of Municipal Affairs by April

15 of the fiscal year that it was adopted. [S150(3)]

Water and Sewer Services

In 2023, the average residential customer paid $636.07 for water and sewer services for the year. With a 3% increase. We anticipate the average residential customer will pay $655.15 for the year. This is an increase of $19.08 annually, or $0.05 daily.

facts.body:

About the City of Charlottetown

Charlottetown, the capital city of Prince Edward Island, is known as the “Birthplace of Confederation” due to the historic 1864 Charlottetown Conference, which set the stage for Confederation.

It is recognized as the unceded territory of the Indigenous Mi'kmaq People.

Charlottetown serves as the seat of the PEI government and is a vibrant hub of culture and education, home to two post-secondary institutions, the University of Prince Edward Island and Holland College.

With a growing knowledge economy and strategic location, Charlottetown attracts global businesses across sectors such as biotechnology, financial services, information technology and manufacturing. Supported by a skilled workforce and a favorable business environment, these industries drive economic growth and innovation.

Offering an exceptional quality of life, Charlottetown combines big-city amenities with cultural events and recreational opportunities in a safe, clean environment that fosters a strong sense of community. As a port city, Charlottetown is a major tourism destination and designated Cultural Capital of Canada, hosting year-round attractions, including the renowned Charlottetown Festival, that takes place in the Confederation Centre of the Arts, located in the heart of our downtown.

Our City also serves as a premier venue for meetings and conventions and has become a leading sport tourism destination, featuring state-of-the-art facilities and hosting major sporting events throughout the year.

With its rich history, vibrant culture, thriving economy and outstanding quality of life, Charlottetown continues to attract residents, businesses, visitors and sports enthusiasts from around the world.

Land Acknowledgement

In the spirit of Reconciliation, we acknowledge that the land upon which we gather is unceded Mi’kmaq territory. Epekwitk (Prince Edward Island), Mi’kma’ki, is covered by the historic Treaties of Peace and Friendship. We pay our respects to the Indigenous Mi’kmaq People who have occupied this Island for over 12,000 years; past, present and future.

Legislative Framework

The City of Charlottetown engages in a comprehensive budget preparation process to allocate resources effectively. In doing so the City must adhere to the Municipal Government Act of Prince Edward Island (the Act) and the Financial Plan Regulations (the Regulations). The Act and Regulations set out the rules for how the City must handle its money, including budgeting, planning for future expenses, and keeping track of assets. The legislation refers to the City budget as a Financial Plan.

Key legislative requirements from the Act:

The fiscal year for the City is April 1 to March 31 [S149(1)]

On or before March 31 in each year, City Council shall by resolution adopt a budget for the upcoming fiscal year. [S150(1)]

City Council must provide public notice and hold a public meeting regarding the budget not less than two weeks before it receives final approval and is adopted. [S151(1)]

A copy of the final approved budget shall be filed with the Minister of Municipal Affairs by

April 15 of the fiscal year that it was adopted. [S150(4)]

Budget Basics

Each year, the City updates its Financial Plan and goes through a budget process to determine how much it will need to spend in the upcoming fiscal year:

Maintain current levels of service (base operating budget)

Incorporate service level enhancements or reductions

Incorporate new operating initiatives

Fund Capital Projects

This Financial Plan includes the Operational Budget and Capital Budget for:

City of Charlottetown

Charlottetown Water and Sewer

Water and Sewer Services

In 2024, the average residential customer paid $655.15 for water and sewer services for the year. With a 2.2 per cent increase this year, we anticipate the average residential customer will pay $669.56 in 2025. This amounts to an increase of $14.41 annually, or four cents a day.

Charlottetown Police Services (CPS) is the municipal police force responsible for public safety, law enforcement, and crime prevention in the capital city. As the largest urban centre in the province, Charlottetown faces unique policing challenges due to its role as a government, tourism, and commercial hub. The city experiences significant population fluctuations due to seasonal tourism, post-secondary institutions, and large-scale events, placing added demands on police resources.

CPS operates with growing challenges and expectations, providing a range of services, including uniformed patrol, criminal investigations, street crime suppression, tactical intelligence, and community outreach. The service also supports policing partners through initiatives like the E-Watch public safety camera system and digital forensics.

With increasing calls for service, rapid population growth, and evolving crime trends driven by technology, CPS is focusing on strategic growth to ensure public safety. While their services are specific to the City of Charlottetown, they also work in collaboration with all other island police agencies.

facts.title: About Charlottetown and land acknowledgement
facts.body:
Charlottetown is the capital city of Prince Edward Island and a growing coastal community home to approximately 48,700 residents. The Greater Capital Region and surrounding area has a population of approximately 96,500 and makes up over half of the Island’s total population. Known as the “Birthplace of Confederation,” Charlottetown hosted the 1864 Charlottetown Conference, which played a pivotal role in the formation of Canada.

The Epekwitnewag Mi’kmaq have occupied Epekwitk (Prince Edward Island) for over 12,000 years, long before the arrival of English, Scottish, Irish, and Acadian settlers throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Today, Charlottetown is home to an increasingly diverse and multicultural population from around the world.

As the beating heart of the Island, Charlottetown’s economy is strongly influenced by the public sector, alongside established industries such as retail trade and tourism. The city is also home to several global companies in the knowledge-based economy and is the regional hub for emerging and high-growth sectors, including bioscience, information and communications technology, and advanced manufacturing and food processing.

Charlottetown is a vibrant tourism destination, attracting over 1.6 million visitors annually, driven by leisure tourism, sport and business event hosting, and cruise arrivals. As a premier event host city, residents and visitors benefit from a lively year-round calendar of festivals and events.

Characterized by historic Victorian architecture, a bustling waterfront boardwalk, a vibrant arts and culture scene, and a reputation for world-class local dining, Charlottetown is widely recognized as an attractive place to live, work and visit. Residents enjoy a safe, walkable city and a high quality of life, supported by proximity to nature, strong community connections, and a wide range of educational, recreational and cultural amenities. Charlottetown is consistently ranked among national and international publications as an affordable place to live and an ideal location to start or grow a business.

Land Acknowledgement

In the spirit of Reconciliation, we acknowledge that the land upon which we gather is unceded Mi’kmaq territory. Epekwitk (Prince Edward Island), Mi’kma’ki, is covered by the historic Treaties of Peace and Friendship. We pay our respects to the Indigenous Mi’kmaq People who have occupied this Island for over 12,000 years; past, present and future.

The Budgeting Process

Municipal operating and capital budgets are done on an annual basis. Baseline operating budgets are prepared by each department looking at past, current, and forecasted expenses. Utilities are self-funded by user rates charged to customers and not funded by general municipal taxes. Utility rates are structured to maintain cost recovery for operations and capital projects. The City of Charlottetown engages in a comprehensive budget preparation process to allocate resources effectively. In doing so, the City must adhere to the Municipal Government Act of Prince Edward Island (the Act) and the Financial Plan Regulations (the Regulations). The Act and Regulations set out the rules for how the City must handle its money, including budgeting, planning for future expenses, and keeping track of assets. facts.title: Capital-city context and service pressures
facts.body:
Capital City Context and Service Pressures

As the provincial capital and largest municipality in Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown plays a central role in the Island’s economic, administrative, and cultural life. This role brings unique opportunities, but also distinct service and infrastructure challenges.

Historic Population Growth

Charlottetown’s population is approximately 48,700 residents. However, the broader Capital Region, which includes the neighbouring towns of Stratford and Cornwall and surrounding rural areas, has a population of roughly 96,500 people and accounts for more than half of PEI’s total population. As the Island’s primary employment, education, government, and service centre, Charlottetown supports not only its residents but also a much larger regional population that rely on the city’s infrastructure and municipal services each day.

Daytime Population and Regional Service Demand

Charlottetown experiences a significant daily influx of workers, students, and visitors. While the city’s infrastructure is funded primarily through municipal property taxes paid by Charlottetown residents and businesses, it serves a population that extends well beyond municipal boundaries.

Traffic data illustrates the scale of this regional demand. In 2023, the average daily traffic volume at the five major access points into Charlottetown totaled approximately 107,414 vehicles per day. The Capital Region population is nearly double that of the city proper, indicating the significant number of commuters and service users who rely on Charlottetown’s road network, transit system, public spaces, and emergency services.

Many of these users reside outside city limits and do not contribute to municipal revenues through property taxes. At the same time, the costs associated with maintaining and expanding infrastructure have increased significantly, while municipal revenue tools have not evolved at the same pace as service demands.

Tourism and Seasonal Population Growth

Charlottetown also serves as one of PEI’s primary tourism gateways. The city welcomes visitors by air, land, and sea, and is home to one of Atlantic Canada’s busiest cruise ports.

The Port of Charlottetown expects nearly 80 cruise ship calls in 2026, bringing an estimated +165,000 visitors to the city. This influx contributes to the local economy and supports businesses, cultural attractions, and hospitality services. At the same time, it places additional seasonal demand on municipal infrastructure and services, including policing and emergency response, water and wastewater systems, traffic management, and the maintenance of parks, streets, and public spaces.

Charlottetown also serves as one of PEI’s primary tourism gateways. The city welcomes visitors by air, land, and sea, and is home to one of Atlantic Canada’s busiest cruise ports.

The Port of Charlottetown expects nearly 80 cruise ship calls in 2026, bringing an estimated +165,000 visitors to the city. This influx contributes to the local economy and supports businesses, cultural attractions, and hospitality services. At the same time, it places additional seasonal demand on municipal infrastructure and services, including policing and emergency response, water and wastewater systems, traffic management, and the maintenance of parks, streets, and public spaces.

facts.title: Service demand and infrastructure pressures
facts.body:
Population growth and regional service demand have also contributed to increased use of municipal services.

Public transit usage has grown significantly since the service was launched in 2015. In 2025, T3 Transit recorded 1.4 million rides, compared with 403,683 rides in its first year of operation. This growth reflects the increasing importance of transit in supporting mobility within the city and across the Capital Region.

Emergency services have also experienced rising demand. Between 2020 and 2024:

Calls for service to Charlottetown Police Services increased by 35%

Charlottetown Fire Department calls increased by 42.8%

These increases reflect both population growth and the city’s role as the primary service centre for much of the Island.

Infrastructure Pressures

Like many municipalities across Atlantic Canada, Charlottetown’s core infrastructure—including water and wastewater systems—was originally constructed to serve a much smaller population than the city supports today.

Maintaining, upgrading and expanding this infrastructure to meet current and future demand represents one of the city’s most significant long-term financial responsibilities.

Moving Toward Sustainable Funding Solutions

These challenges are not unique to Charlottetown but are common among capital cities and regional service hubs. Recognizing this, the City of Charlottetown continues to work with the Federation of Prince Edward Island Municipalities and other local governments in advocating for a more equitable, long-term funding framework that reflects the realities of modern municipal service delivery.

Strengthening collaboration with provincial and federal partners will be essential to ensuring that Charlottetown can continue to provide the infrastructure and services required to support residents, businesses, and visitors—while sustaining the city’s role as the capital and economic centre of PEI.

facts.title: Funding and taxation in Charlottetown
facts.body:
Funding & Taxation

Sources of Funding

The City receives funding for services and capital projects from the following sources:

Property taxes

Provincial/federal grants

Water and Sewer service fees

User fees

Tax Collection & Revenue Sharing

How Property Taxes Work in Charlottetown

Property taxes for Charlottetown are collected and administered by the Government of Prince Edward Island. The province is responsible for billing and collecting municipal property taxes, provincial property taxes, provincial income taxes, as well as fire and waste management charges. The municipal portion of property tax revenue is then remitted to the City on a monthly basis. These municipal revenues support core local services, including policing, fire protection, public transit, and infrastructure maintenance and renewal.

Water and Sewer utility fees are collected and managed directly by the City and are funded separately from property taxes.

Assessment

Property assessments are conducted annually by the province. Assessment notices and property tax bills are typically issued in early May.

Rate Setting

Each March, City Council establishes the municipal property tax rate as part of the annual budgeting process. The current municipal residential rate is $0.67 per $100 of assessed value. This rate is applied in addition to the provincial rate of $1.50 per $100 of assessed value, which includes a $0.50 residential credit.

Revenue Sharing with the Province

Under the current structure, the province collects all property taxes and remits the municipal portion to the City. Across PEI, municipalities — including Charlottetown — receive approximately 2.2 cents of every property tax dollar collected. By comparison, municipalities across Canada typically receive between 8 and 10 cents per property tax dollar collected. In addition to property tax revenues, Charlottetown receives provincial transfers that help support important services and programs that residents rely on.

The City continues to engage with the Province on revenue-sharing arrangements, with the goal of achieving a more equitable and sustainable revenue-sharing model to help the city address increased infrastructure demands, public safety costs, and population growth pressures.

facts.title: Innovation Task Force
facts.body:
In September 2025, Charlottetown’s Chief Administrative Officer (CAO) Brad MacConnell

launched the Innovation Task Force – a cross-departmental working group tasked with improving how technology, data, and business practices are aligned across City departments. The task force brings together staff from across the organization to identify opportunities where new tools, improved processes and data sharing can enhance the way the City operates and serves residents.

A key focus of the task force is identifying practical ways to deliver services more efficiently, while maintaining and improving service levels. By reviewing existing policies, reducing duplication, and exploring the use of modern digital tools, the task force is working to find operational efficiencies that reduce costs without compromising the high quality programs and services residents rely on.

The Innovation Task Force is an important part of the City’s ongoing commitment to modernizing municipal operations. By proactively seeking efficiencies and smarter ways of working, the City is positioning itself to manage costs responsibly and ensuring resources are used as effectively as possible.

facts.title: Charlottetown Police Services: Department Summary
facts.body:
Charlottetown Police Services (CPS) is the municipal police force responsible for public safety, law enforcement, and crime prevention in the capital city. As the largest urban centre in the province, Charlottetown faces unique policing challenges due to its role as a government, tourism, and commercial hub. The city experiences significant population fluctuations due to seasonal tourism, post-secondary institutions, and large-scale events, placing added demands on police resources.

CPS provides a range of services, including uniformed patrol, major crime investigations, street crime countermeasures, forensic identification, tactical response, traffic and road safety, and community outreach. The department also supports policing partners and other PEI communities through initiatives like the E-Watch public safety camera system and digital forensics.

With increasing calls for service, rapid population growth, and evolving crime trends driven by technology, CPS is focusing on strategic growth to ensure public safety. As the largest urban centre in the province, Charlottetown faces unique policing challenges due to its role as a government, tourism, and commercial hub. The city experiences significant population fluctuations due to seasonal tourism, post-secondary institutions, and large-scale events, placing added demands on police resources.

CPS provides a range of services, including uniformed patrol, major crime investigations, street crime countermeasures, forensic identification, tactical response, traffic and road safety, and community outreach. The department also supports policing partners and other PEI communities through initiatives like the E-Watch public safety camera system and digital forensics.

With increasing calls for service, rapid population growth, and evolving crime trends driven by technology, CPS is focusing on strategic growth to ensure public safety. With the introduction of provincial policing standards in December 2025, a key area of focus for CPS over the next two years will be to further review and adequately address the new standards at the local level.

facts.title: Charlottetown Water and Sewer: Department Summary
facts.body:
The Water and Sewer Utility is responsible for providing safe, clean water to residents and businesses in Charlottetown. It manages the overall water system, pumps and storage facilities that bring water from the watershed into the City system.

The Utility also operates the Charlottetown Pollution Control Plant, also known as Wastewater Treatment Plant, which manages the collection and treatment system for all wastewater in Charlottetown.
